extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in the herbicide Roundup/glyphosate and its health, environmental, regulatory, and legal aspects
extracted.subtask_description: A general encyclopedia article summarizing the composition, toxicology, environmental effects, regulatory classifications, legal history, advertising disputes, and agricultural uses of the Roundup brand of herbicides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition / active ingredients and adjuvants
rubrics_metrics.description: The main active ingredient of Roundup is the isopropylamine salt of glyphosate; glyphosate-based formulations may contain a number of adjuvants, the identities of which may be proprietary. Polyethoxylated tallow amine (POEA) is a surfactant used in the original Roundup formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different versions include different percentages of POEA and other adjuvants; non-glyphosate Roundup formulations may use MCPA, quinclorac, dicamba, sulfentrazone, penoxsulam, or 2,4-D. Because adjuvants can be proprietary and formulations vary (five different glyphosate salts and different inert ingredients), assessing product properties requires knowing the specific formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acute toxicity (formulation-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lethal dose of different glyphosate-based formulations varies, especially with respect to the surfactants used; formulations intended for terrestrial use that include the surfactant POEA can be more toxic than other formulations for aquatic species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because formulations vary widely, it is difficult to determine the contribution of surfactants to overall toxicity for each product. Empirical toxicology must account for the exact formulation and surfactant content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human acute health effects and routes of exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Acute oral toxicity for mammals is low but deaths have occurred after deliberate overdose of concentrated Roundup; concentrated ingestion (85–200 ml of 41% solution) has resulted in death within hours in some cases. Skin exposure can cause irritation and rarely severe burns; inhalation is a minor route but spray mist can irritate throat; eye exposure may cause conjunctivitis or corneal injury if not promptly irrigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severity depends on concentration and quantity ingested; surfactants can increase relative acute toxicity. Regulatory risk assessments and clinical case reports should be consulted for treatment and classification of human exposures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin and eye irritation data limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is very limited information on skin irritation in humans; available human data was insufficient to support classification for skin corrosion or irritation (per ECHA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where skin irritation has been reported it is unclear whether glyphosate or co-formulants are responsible. Risk classification may therefore rely on limited or ambiguous human data and on animal studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aquatic organism toxicity and aquatic-use restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Glyphosate formulations with POEA, such as Roundup, are not approved for aquatic use due to aquatic organism toxicity; terrestrial formulations containing POEA and MON 0818 may have negative impacts on protozoa, mussels, crustaceans, frogs, and fish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Environmental risk to aquatic organisms arises from drift or temporary water pockets; although laboratory studies can show effects, such observations rarely occur in the field when herbicide label instructions are followed. Assessment must consider likelihood of aquatic exposure and formulation-specific toxicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amphibian impacts and developmental effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies in amphibians have shown toxicity of products containing POEA to amphibian larvae: interference with gill morphology, mortality via osmotic instability or asphyxiation, delayed or accelerated development, reduced size at metamorphosis, developmental malformations, histological indications of intersex, and oxidative stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although observed in laboratory studies, glyphosate-based pesticides are not considered the major cause of amphibian decline globally; risk assessments should consider exposure context and field relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on bees and pollinators
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain Roundup formulations (Roundup Ready-To-Use, Roundup No Glyphosate, Roundup ProActive) have been found to cause significant mortality in bumblebees when sprayed directly on them; surfactants are hypothesized to block bees' tracheal systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct spray exposure to foraging bees is a high-risk scenario; assessments should distinguish direct contact vs. indirect/field exposure and consider formulation surfactants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carcinogenicity evidence and agency classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: There is limited evidence that human cancer risk might increase as a result of occupational exposure to large amounts of glyphosate, but no good evidence of such a risk from home use; most national pesticide regulatory agencies and scientific organizations have concluded labeled uses show no evidence of human carcinogenicity. However, IARC classified glyphosate as Group 2A 'probably carcinogenic to humans' in 2015.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification varies across agencies (EPA classifications changed over time from Group C to Group E to 'Not Likely to be Carcinogenic'); variation is attributed to differences in datasets and evaluation methodology. Risk conclusions should therefore state which agency's assessment is cited and acknowledge methodological differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational vs. consumer exposure distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The article distinguishes between occupational exposure (large amounts in agricultural work), where limited evidence of increased cancer risk exists, and home/domestic use, where there is no good evidence of such a risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk communication and regulatory decisions should separately evaluate high-exposure occupational scenarios and low-exposure consumer scenarios; exposure magnitude and frequency are key determinants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory risk assessment conclusions and caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent scientific reviews and regulatory agencies have repeatedly concluded glyphosate-based herbicides do not lead to a significant risk for human or environmental health when the product label is properly followed. Some reviews concluded minimal acute and chronic risk predicted for terrestrial non-target organisms but noted some risks to aquatic organisms in shallow water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions depend on labeled use and adherence to instructions; risk assessments should document assumptions about exposure, formulation, and environmental pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label adherence and field relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: While laboratory studies can show effects of glyphosate formulations on aquatic organisms, similar observations rarely occur in the field when instructions on the herbicide label are followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory and environmental impact evaluations should account for real-world use patterns and label compliance; laboratory toxicity does not automatically imply field-level harm without plausible exposure pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal liability: failure-to-warn theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Most cases claiming injury from Roundup are based on a failure-to-warn theory of liability — that Monsanto/Bayer failed to warn plaintiffs that Roundup can cause cancer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal outcomes hinge on what the company knew, what warnings were provided, preemption questions under FIFRA, and conflicting appellate decisions across circuits. Litigation risk assessment should consider jurisdictional differences and evolving case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption/legal conflict regarding FIFRA
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate courts have conflicted on whether state-law failure-to-warn claims are preempted by the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA); Ninth and Eleventh Circuits held such claims not preempted, while the Third Circuit held FIFRA does preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This circuit split raises the potential for Supreme Court review; legal strategy and risk evaluation must track prevailing jurisdictional precedent and potential changes at the national level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation outcomes and settlements as risk indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Bayer (which acquired Monsanto) agreed to pay billions to settle tens of thousands of claims alleging Roundup caused cancer; settlements, jury verdicts (later reduced or reversed on appeal), and ongoing pending claims are part of the product's legal history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement amounts and case outcomes provide information about litigation exposure but do not themselves resolve scientific causation; interpretation should separate legal resolutions from scientific consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: False advertising and marketing claims scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Monsanto faced lawsuits and convictions alleging false or misleading advertising that Roundup products were 'practically non-toxic', 'environmentally friendly', or 'biodegradable'; settlements required removing claims or paying damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product labeling and advertising claims should be substantiated by data and consistent with regulatory classifications; history of advertising disputes is relevant to consumer trust and compliance risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredient transparency affecting risk assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjuvants' identities may be proprietary, which complicates determining how much surfactants contribute to overall toxicity of each formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory review and independent science may be hampered by lack of full ingredient disclosure; assessments should note proprietary limitations and, where possible, test whole formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use with genetically engineered (Roundup Ready) crops
rubrics_metrics.description: Monsanto produced seeds genetically engineered to be tolerant to glyphosate (Roundup Ready), allowing farmers to use glyphosate as a post-emergence herbicide against most broadleaf and cereal weeds; these genes were patented and helped drive rapid growth in Roundup sales after 1996.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of agricultural impacts should consider the interaction between herbicide use and GM crop adoption (e.g., usage patterns, selection for resistant weeds, economic effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Market and patent context
rubrics_metrics.description: Monsanto patented the herbicidal use of glyphosate; U.S. patent exclusivity ended in 2000 and similar products now use glyphosate as an active ingredient; the Roundup trademark remains registered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent expiry and trademark status affect market competition, availability of formulations, and the economics of litigation and regulatory compliance; assessments of product prevalence should consider patent and market history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory bans and national court actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include France banning Roundup Pro 360 after a court found the regulator had not given due weight to safety concerns; national regulatory and judicial actions have led to product bans or annulments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country-specific regulatory and judicial outcomes can differ; risk and compliance evaluations must be jurisdiction-aware and consider local court findings and regulatory processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-source heterogeneity and methodological differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation in agency classifications (e.g., IARC vs. other national agencies) has been attributed to 'use of different data sets' and 'methodological differences in the evaluation of the available evidence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When synthesizing evidence, explicitly note dataset choices, study inclusion/exclusion, and evaluation methods; transparently report which assessments are being referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecosystem-scale risk versus laboratory findings
rubrics_metrics.description: While laboratory studies show toxic effects on various organisms, the use patterns, exposure probabilities, and ecological context mean field effects are often less pronounced when labels are followed; some reviews still predict risks to certain aquatic or non-target organisms under specific exposure scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk characterization should bridge lab-to-field extrapolation carefully, using exposure modeling, real-world monitoring data, and consideration of label-compliant practices.
